passages.t: Not yet time? Consider your ways
passages.happening:
‘In the second year of the reign of Darius, on the first day of the sixth month, the word of the LORD came through Haggai the prophet’ (verse 1) to Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest. The people say the time has not yet come to rebuild the LORD's house (verse 2). ‘Is it a time for you yourselves to live in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?’ (verse 4).

‘Consider carefully your ways’ (verse 5). They have planted much and harvested little, eaten and drunk and never been satisfied, ‘You earn wages to put into a bag pierced through’ (verse 6). They are to go up into the hills, bring down timber and build the house, so that God may take pleasure in it and be glorified (verse 8). They expected much and got little, because God's house lies in ruins while each of them is busy with his own (verse 9). So the heavens have held back their dew, and God has called a drought on the land (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
The date is late August 520 BC. Darius I had seized the Persian throne in 522 BC after the death of Cambyses, son of Cyrus, and spent his first years putting down revolts, recorded in a great inscription on the cliff at Behistun in western Iran. By 520 his rule was secure. Judah was a small province in the Persian region called Beyond the River, led by a governor, Zerubbabel, and a high priest, Joshua. Zerubbabel was a descendant of David, a grandson of King Jehoiachin, who had been taken to Babylon in 597 BC.

For the returned exiles, a rebuilt temple would mean that God was again present among them and their life as his people had truly begun again. Neighbors would have read a ruined temple as a sign that the God of Israel was weak or absent. Paneled houses were a mark of comfort; paneling with cedar was linked with royal buildings.

The people's excuse sounds reasonable: times were hard. Haggai turns it around. Times were hard because they had put God's house last.
passages.later: Ezra tells how the work stopped (Ezra 4:24) and how Haggai and Zechariah stirred it again (Ezra 5:1-2). The law had warned of drought for a people who turned from God (Deuteronomy 28:23-24).
passages.hard:
Does Haggai teach that economic hardship is always God's punishment for neglecting religious duties?

Haggai links the community's failed harvests directly to their neglect of the temple, and some readers have turned this into a general rule: if you are struggling with money, you must be disobeying God, and if you give to God's work, you will prosper. Most interpreters think that misreads the book. Haggai speaks a particular prophetic word to a particular community under the covenant of Sinai, whose warnings were tied to life in the land. The rest of Scripture resists a universal formula: Job suffers though righteous, the psalmists see the wicked prosper, and Jesus rejects the assumption that suffering always reflects a particular sin (John 9:1-3).

The book gives no one a rule that poverty is punishment, and no promise that giving buys prosperity. What it does ask is whether God's purposes come first in a person's life.
passages.asks: The people said it was not yet time to build God's house, while finishing their own. Ask what you have been putting off for God until things are easier. And ask where you have been earning wages into a bag with holes.

passages.t: The people obey, and the work begins
passages.happening:
Zerubbabel, Joshua and all the remnant of the people obeyed the voice of the LORD and the words of Haggai, and they feared the LORD (verse 12). Haggai, the LORD's messenger, gives the people the LORD's message: “I am with you,” declares the LORD (verse 13).

The LORD stirred the spirit of Zerubbabel, the spirit of Joshua and the spirit of all the remnant, and they came and began work on the house of the LORD of Hosts, their God (verse 14), ‘on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Many prophets were ignored. Haggai was heard. Within twenty-four days of his first message, the leaders and the people were at work.

The order matters. They obeyed and feared the LORD. God answered with the shortest promise in the book: he is with them. Then he stirred their spirits, and they began. The same God who rebuked them gave them the will to do what he asked.

Haggai is called the LORD's messenger, a title used for prophets and priests who carry God's word. The returned exiles are called the remnant, the survivors God had kept.
passages.later: Ezra records the same event: ‘Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem’ (Ezra 5:2). God had stirred Cyrus's spirit in the same way to send the exiles home (Ezra 1:1).
passages.asks: The people obeyed, and God said he was with them. Ask what step of obedience is in front of you. And ask what it would mean to let God stir your spirit for work you have been avoiding.
